title: Bind git correlation engine through the bridge
description:
Bind bv's `pkg/correlation` through the engine bridge so bvx can link beads to
commits.

The engine work is mostly exposure rather than new logic — bv already scores
links by explicit reference, co-commit pattern, file overlap and temporal
proximity, and maintains incremental per-commit disk caches.

**Scope**

- New bridge methods: `history`, `causality`, `file_beads`, `file_hotspots`,
  `file_relations`, `orphans`, `related`, `impact_network`
- Swift models for the correlation payloads
- Confidence scores surfaced, never rounded away

**Watch out**

`pkg/correlation/gitcmd.go` shells out to `git`, which the App Sandbox forbids.
Route the sandboxed app through direct object-store reads; the CLI can keep the
subprocess path. This is the one place the design doc expects an
upstream-friendly patch.
close_reason: Correlation bound via object store; flow and attention views shipped

title: Markdown tables are not rendered in the description
description:
`MarkdownParser` has no table support, so a pipe table in a description is
mangled. Verified against the real parser:

```
input:  | Metric | Value |
        |---|---|
        | PageRank | 0.20 |

parsed: paragraph("| Metric | Value | |---|---| | PageRank | 0.20 |")
```

Two distinct symptoms depending on the rest of the text:

- **Table alone** — `looksLikeMarkdown` returns `false`, so the description
  renders verbatim. Rows survive but show as literal pipes in body font.
- **Table beside any other Markdown** — detection fires, the rows fall through
  to the paragraph branch, and `joinSoftWrapped` collapses every row onto a
  single line. This is the bad one, and it is a side effect of the soft-break
  fix: correct for prose, destructive for tables.

**Scope**

- `MarkdownBlock.table(headers:rows:alignments:)`
- Recognise a header row followed by a delimiter row (`|---|:--:|---:|`),
  including the leading/trailing-pipe-optional forms
- Render with SwiftUI `Grid`, honouring column alignment, inline spans per cell,
  and horizontal scroll when the table is wider than the inspector
- Add `|` as a detection signal *only* when a delimiter row follows, so prose
  containing a stray pipe is not misread

**Tests**

Parser cases for aligned/unaligned, ragged rows (fewer cells than headers),
tables with inline code in cells, and a false-positive guard for prose like
`use a | b to pipe`. Plus a render snapshot.
close_reason: Markdown tables parse and render; regression tests added

title: Make bead ids in the detail view clickable
description:
In the detail pane, a bead id mentioned in prose should be clickable and select
that bead.

Today the **Dependencies** section links beads, but an id inside the
description, notes or a comment is inert text. Descriptions routinely say things
like "work on bvx-8ou first to unblock this", and following that reference means
finding it manually in the list.

**Scope**

- Detect ids matching the workspace prefix plus `br`'s minted token
  (`bvx-8ou`, `bvx-v49`, and the longer forms), taken from the store's
  configured `issue_prefix` rather than hardcoded
- Render each as a link that sets `store.selection`
- Apply in the description, and in comment bodies
- **Only link ids that exist in the loaded workspace.** An unknown or stale id
  stays plain text — a link that selects nothing is worse than no link
- Show the target's title on hover

**Design note**

This interacts with the Markdown work: linkification has to run on the inline
span *after* `AttributedString` parsing, or it will corrupt ids that appear
inside fenced code and inline code, where they must stay literal.
close_reason: Bead ids in descriptions and comments link to their bead

title: Sort the issue list from its column headers
description:
Sort the issue list by clicking its column headers, the way every native macOS
table does, instead of only through the toolbar's Sort dropdown.

**Scope**

- Move `IssueListView` to SwiftUI `Table`'s `sortOrder:` binding with
  `TableColumn(_, value:)`, which gives clickable headers and the direction
  chevron for free
- Keep the toolbar menu — it stays the discoverable path and is where
  non-column orderings live

**Two constraints that are easy to get wrong**

- **Metric columns must stay disabled until Phase 2 lands.** Sorting by PageRank
  before it is computed would order by absent values. The existing
  `hasPhase2Values` gate has to cover the header path too, not just the menu.
- **bv's `s` key cycles sort modes**, and the terminal-keys layer still binds it.
  Header clicks and the cycle must drive the same state, or the two disagree
  about what the current order is.

**Tests**

Header-driven ordering for each column, a metric column staying inert before
Phase 2, and agreement between the header state and `SortMode`.
close_reason: Column headers sort the list, sharing one sort state with the toolbar and the s cycle

title: Multi-selection in the issue list
description:
Let the list select more than one bead at a time, the way every native macOS
table does.

**Scope**

- Move `store.selection` from `Issue.ID?` to `Set<Issue.ID>`, which is what
  SwiftUI `Table`'s `selection:` binding takes for multi-select
- Shift-click for a range, Command-click to add or remove one

**What the change ripples into**

`selection` is read in a lot of places that assume exactly one bead, and each
needs a decision rather than a mechanical fix:

- **The inspector** shows one bead. With several selected it should show the
  most recently added one or a summary of the set — showing the first silently
  hides that more are selected.
- **`selectedIssue` and `select(id:)`** are single-bead helpers used by the
  inline bead-id links, the `bvx://` URL scheme, Spotlight activation, the flow
  matrix drilldown, the alerts panel and the sprint critical path. All of those
  should still end up with exactly one bead selected — replacing the selection
  rather than extending it.
- **bv's `j`/`k` bindings** move a single cursor. They should keep doing that,
  which means the terminal-keys layer needs a notion of "the focused bead"
  distinct from "the selected set".

**Tests**

A shift-click range, that `select(id:)` replaces rather than extends, that the
inspector does something defensible with two selected, and that `j`/`k` still
move one cursor.
close_reason: Implemented: multi-selection with a derived focus, a selection-sensitive context menu with Copy ID, and an Open-panel guard backed by the new bvx_probe entry point

title: Context menu on the issue list, starting with Copy ID
description:
Right-clicking a row should offer actions, and those actions should know how
many beads they apply to.

**Scope**

- `.contextMenu(forSelectionType: Issue.ID.self)` on the `Table`. This is the
  API that matches the requirement exactly: SwiftUI hands the closure the set
  the menu applies to — the current selection when the right-clicked row is
  part of it, otherwise just that row. So "the selected beads, or the hovered
  one when it is not in the selection" falls out of the framework rather than
  having to be reconstructed from mouse position.
- First item: **Copy ID**. One bead copies its id; several copy the ids joined
  with `", "`.
- Build the menu so it can carry more items later, with distinct zero-, one-
  and many-selection variants from the start.

**Watch out**

- **The empty case is real.** Right-clicking the table's background yields an
  empty set. The menu should degrade to workspace-level items, or to nothing —
  not to a Copy ID that puts an empty string on the clipboard.
- **Order the joined ids by what is on screen**, not by `Set` iteration, which
  is unordered. Otherwise copying the same selection twice can produce two
  different strings.

**Tests**

One selected, several selected — asserting both the `", "` separator and a
stable order — and the empty case putting nothing on the pasteboard.
close_reason: Implemented: multi-selection with a derived focus, a selection-sensitive context menu with Copy ID, and an Open-panel guard backed by the new bvx_probe entry point

title: Only offer folders that hold bead data in the open panel
description:
The Open panel accepts any folder, so a folder with no bead data fails only
after it has been chosen. `NSOpenPanel`'s delegate can disable the ones that
cannot work, making the mistake unavailable rather than reported.

**Scope**

- `NSOpenPanelDelegate.panel(_:shouldEnable:)`, returning false for a directory
  the engine could not open

**The rule is not simply "contains .beads"**

`resolveSource` accepts several shapes, and a naive check would disable things
that work today:

- a folder containing `.beads`
- a `.beads` directory chosen directly
- a `.jsonl` or `.db` file chosen directly
- **a multi-repository workspace root**, which holds `.bv/workspace.yaml` while
  its `.beads` directories live in the repositories *below* it. Requiring
  `.beads` at the chosen level would make every workspace root unselectable.
  This is the case most likely to be missed, and it would silently undo
  bvx-e3y.
- a folder *below* one containing `.beads`, since discovery walks upwards

**Keep one copy of the rule**

Whatever predicate is written should be derived from the engine's discovery
rules rather than being a second implementation of them in Swift. Two copies
will drift, and the symptom — a folder that the panel refuses but the CLI opens
happily — is confusing enough to be worth designing out.

**Tests**

Each accepted shape above enables; a folder with no bead data anywhere above or
below it does not; and a workspace root with `.bv/workspace.yaml` enables.
close_reason: Implemented: multi-selection with a derived focus, a selection-sensitive context menu with Copy ID, and an Open-panel guard backed by the new bvx_probe entry point

title: Move the Priority column immediately after the ID column
description:
In `Sources/VBXUI/IssueListView.swift` the `Table` declares columns in the order ID, type glyph (unsorted), Title, Status, P, Blocks, Blocked by, PageRank, Labels, Updated. Priority is a primary triage signal and currently sits past the title and status, so it is easy to miss when scanning.

Move the `TableColumn("P", value: \.priority)` block so it renders immediately after the `TableColumn("ID", value: \.id)` block — ahead of the type glyph, the title and the status.

Only the visual column order changes. `SortColumn`, the `IssueRow` key paths and the header-click sort wiring in the same file stay as they are.

Tests: `Tests/VBXUITests/ColumnHeaderSortTests.swift` and the list snapshot in `Tests/VBXUITests/ViewSnapshotTests.swift` cover this view; add or adjust an assertion that pins the new order so the layout cannot silently drift back.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-implement-open-beads

title: Render list labels as pills instead of a comma-joined string
description:
The Labels column in `Sources/VBXUI/IssueListView.swift` renders `row.issue.labels.joined(separator: ", ")` as one secondary-styled `Text`, so individual labels have no visual boundary and a long list reads as run-on prose truncated at one line.

Render each label as its own pill — a rounded capsule with a background fill, small font and horizontal padding — laid out in an `HStack`, matching the treatment `StatusChip` already gives status in the neighbouring column. Reuse or generalise that chip rather than inventing a second style.

Keep the column single-line: pills that do not fit are clipped, with the full comma-joined list available via `.help()` so nothing becomes unreadable at a narrow width. Sorting is unchanged — `labelsKey` stays the comma-joined lowercased string.

Tests: extend the list snapshot in `Tests/VBXUITests/ViewSnapshotTests.swift` with a bead carrying several labels and assert on ink coverage (per this repo's rule, `NSHostingView`, never `ImageRenderer`).
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-implement-open-beads

title: Make linked bead ids look and feel clickable
description:
`MarkdownText.linkBeadReferences` (`Sources/VBXUI/MarkdownText.swift:208`) sets `attributed[range].link = BeadURL.open(bead:)` and a tooltip, but nothing else. A linked id is therefore visually indistinguishable from the prose around it, and the mouse pointer stays an I-beam over it, so there is no cue that it is clickable at all.

Two changes, both scoped to the linked range:

1. **Tint the range** so linked ids stand out from body text — a distinct accent colour, applied alongside the existing `.link` attribute. Only ids the workspace actually holds are linked (a stale id is deliberately left as plain text), so the tint doubles as a signal that the target exists.
2. **Show a pointing-hand cursor on hover.** `.pointerStyle(.link)` is macOS 15 and this package targets `.macOS(.v14)` (`Package.swift:22`), so use `onContinuousHover` with `NSCursor.pointingHand` push/pop. Balance the push and pop on exit — a leaked push leaves the cursor wrong across the whole window.

The hover region must follow the linked range, not the whole `Text`, or the cursor changes over unlinked prose too.

Tests: `Tests/VBXUITests/BeadLinkRenderTests.swift` already asserts on the attributed output — extend it to cover the colour attribute on exactly the linked ranges, and to confirm an unknown id gets neither link nor tint.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-implement-open-beads

title: Add back and forward navigation through a 20-entry view history
description:
There is no way back to where you just were. `store.surface` (`Sources/VBXAppCore/ProjectStore.swift:103`) and `store.selection` (line 111) are each overwritten in place, so switching surface or following a bead link discards the previous position with no way to return — which is most costly exactly where the app invites wandering, following bead links between beads.

**History.** Keep the last 20 visited entries in `ProjectStore`, oldest evicted first. An entry is a view position: the `ViewSurface` plus the selected bead, since following a bead link changes selection without changing surface and is a navigation step the user will expect to undo.

**Buttons.** Add back and forward to the *leading* end of the top bar, before the existing view `Picker` at `ContentView.swift:88` (`ToolbarItem(placement: .navigation)`). Icons only, `chevron.left` / `chevron.right` — no words. Give each a `.help()` tooltip, which is the accessible label the glyph alone does not provide.

**Disabled states.** Back is disabled at the oldest entry, forward at the newest; both are disabled when the history holds a single entry. Use `.disabled()` rather than hand-drawn grey so the styling tracks the system.

**The cursor is the part that is easy to get wrong.** Navigating back must move a cursor through the history, not pop the entry — otherwise forward has nothing to return to. A *new* navigation performed while the cursor sits mid-history truncates everything ahead of it, which is what every browser does and what makes forward predictable. Restoring an entry must not itself push a new one, or back becomes a no-op that re-records where you already are.

Tests: a unit test in `Tests/VBXAppCoreTests/ProjectStoreTests.swift` covering the cursor rules directly — cap and eviction at 20, back/forward round trip, truncation of the forward branch on a new navigation, restore not re-recording, and the two disabled edges.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-implement-open-beads

title: Reset all filters to their defaults when a new workspace is opened
description:
`ProjectStore.open(path:)` (`Sources/VBXAppCore/ProjectStore.swift:482`) swaps the workspace — engine open, `refreshAll()`, navigation-history reset, watcher restart, Phase 2 — but leaves every piece of filter state exactly as the previous workspace left it. Opening a second workspace therefore inherits filters chosen for the first one.

The stale state is:

- `query` (`:109`) — `filter`, `searchText`, `labels`, `assignees` and `sort` (`IssueQuery`, `Sources/VBXCore/Filtering.swift:204`).
- `repoFilter` (`:198`) — repository names, narrowed in `narrowToRepos` (`:284`).
- `activeRecipe` / `recipeIDs` / `recipeTruncated` (`:225`–`:228`) — a recipe from the old workspace keeps replacing the filter and sort, and its ids name beads the new workspace does not hold.
- `alertSeverityFilter` / `alertTypeFilter` (`:233`–`:234`), which are passed to the engine on the next alerts load (`:764`).

The label, assignee, repository and recipe values are the damaging ones: they are workspace-specific strings, so after a switch they typically match nothing and the list comes up **empty with no visible cause** — the sidebar shows a filter the user did not choose for this workspace, and an empty table reads as "this workspace has no beads".

The rule is already established twice in this same function; filters are simply the case nobody carried it to:

- `resetNavigationHistory()` (`:493`) is called there with the comment *"Positions name beads, and the previous workspace's beads do not exist in this one."*
- `refreshAll` (`:578`) keeps only selected ids the fresh bead set still holds, falling back to the first visible bead.

A label, an assignee, a repo name and a recipe's ids are workspace-specific in exactly the way a position or a selected id is.

**The change:** reset the state above to its initialiser defaults when opening a *different* workspace — `query = IssueQuery()`, `repoFilter = []`, recipe cleared, alert filters nil — before `refreshAll()`, so the first render is already unfiltered. Sit it next to the `resetNavigationHistory()` call, for the same stated reason.

Reload of the *same* workspace must not reset anything: `reload(force:)` (`:512`) exists to keep the view stable while the file changes underneath, and the watcher calls it on every write.

Scope note: this is about filters. `surface` (`:103`) — which view the user is on — is not a filter, and carrying it across is reasonable; leave it, and say so rather than resetting it silently.

Tests: `Tests/VBXAppCoreTests/ProjectStoreTests.swift`. Set a label filter, a repo filter and a recipe on one fixture workspace, open a second, and assert each is back to its default and the visible list is non-empty. Add the negative half too — a `reload()` on an unchanged workspace preserves the active filter — or a naive reset in `refreshAll` would pass the first test while breaking live reload.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-filter-reset-on-open

title: Open panel: unopenable folders cannot be entered, and every file is selectable
description:
The Open panel cannot be navigated to a workspace unless you already start inside one, and it greys out nothing among files. Two independent defects, both in the guard's `shouldEnable` contract.

## 1. An unopenable folder cannot be entered, so a workspace below it is unreachable

`OpenPanelGuard.panel(_:shouldEnable:)` (`Sources/VBXAppCore/OpenPanelGuard.swift:80`) returns `canOpen(url.path)` for directories as well as files. The type's own documentation says this is safe:

> It is advisory: AppKit still lets the user navigate *into* a disabled directory, which is essential, because the folders on the way to a repository are themselves unopenable.

**That assumption is wrong.** A directory disabled through `shouldEnable` cannot be double-clicked to enter it, so the folders on the way to a repository are dead ends. `/Users/michel/src` holds no `.beads` and none above it, so it probes `can_open=false` — and a user browsing from home cannot get down to `/Users/michel/src/qjam/vbx` at all.

The fix the design already anticipates: **return `true` for every directory** and let `panel(_:validate:)` (`:84`) do the refusing. That hook already exists, already runs on OK, and already throws a reason — its doc comment describes exactly this job for folders typed into the Go-to-folder sheet. Greying should apply to files only.

Selecting an unopenable folder then produces the guard's existing refusal alert rather than a silent no-op, which is a better answer than a row that cannot be reached.

## 2. Every file is selectable, because the probe accepts any file at all

`Probe` (`Engine/bridge/engine/probe.go:51`) delegates to `resolveSource`, whose non-directory branch (`engine.go:99`) returns `(path, "jsonl")` for anything that is not `.db`/`.sqlite`/`.sqlite3` — with no check that the file is bead data, or even text. Measured:

```
PROBE .../README.md      -> can_open=true  kind="jsonl" source=".../README.md"
PROBE .../Package.swift  -> can_open=true  kind="jsonl"
PROBE .../vbx.icns       -> can_open=true  kind="jsonl"   (a binary icon file)
```

So `shouldEnable` returns true for every file on screen and nothing is greyed. Choosing one gets as far as the loader before failing, which is precisely the panel/loader disagreement `Probe`'s own header comment says it exists to design out.

`canChooseFiles = true` (`ProjectStore.swift:469`) is correct and should stay — the engine genuinely opens a `.jsonl` or `.db` chosen directly. What is missing is that the probe should only say yes to a file it would actually read: extension `.jsonl`/`.db`/`.sqlite`/`.sqlite3`, and ideally a cheap sniff that a `.jsonl` parses as bead data rather than trusting the suffix.

Fix this in the engine, not in Swift: the probe and the loader must keep answering from one set of rules, so `resolveSource` is where the file check belongs. Note that tightening it changes what `open` accepts too — that is the point, but it wants a check for callers that pass a bare path.

## Also found, decide whether to fix here

The header comment on `Probe` says discovery "does *not* walk upwards". It does — `loader.GetBeadsDir` searches ancestors:

```
PROBE /Users/michel/src/qjam/vbx/Sources -> can_open=true source=".../vbx/.beads/issues.jsonl"
```

`Sources/` holds no `.beads` yet probes openable and resolves to the repository root's data. Either the comment is wrong or the behaviour is; upward discovery is arguably right (opening any folder in a repo opens that repo) but it is undocumented and it makes the "folder below a workspace root is refused" claim in the same comment false.

## Tests

`Tests/VBXAppCoreTests/OpenPanelGuardTests.swift` for the guard: a folder that cannot be opened must still be *enabled* (so it can be entered) while `validate` throws for it — the two halves are what stop a fix for one from silently breaking the other. Go-side, `Engine/bridge/engine/probe_test.go` for the file rules: a `.md`, a binary, and an extensionless file must all probe `can_open=false`, and a real `.jsonl`/`.db` must stay true.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-panel-and-history

title: Selecting a different bead in the list should record a navigation position
description:
Selecting a different bead in the list leaves the navigation history unchanged, so back does not return to the bead you were just reading.

**This reverses a deliberate choice made in `vbx-8lk`,** and that context matters for whoever implements it. `noteFocusChanged()` (`Sources/VBXAppCore/Navigation.swift:76`) currently *updates the current entry in place* rather than pushing a new one, on this reasoning:

> Moving down the list with `j`/`k` is browsing, not navigation: pushing an entry per row would evict every real position within one screenful.

Only `select(id:)` — a bead link, a board or tree card, a URL — pushes a position. A plain table click or `j`/`k` writes `selection` directly and pushes nothing. The reported behaviour is exactly that rule working as written, and the report says the rule is wrong: viewing a bead *is* a place you were, and back should return to it.

## The change

- **Coalesce a run of selection changes.** Consecutive positions that differ only by bead, recorded within a short window, collapse into one entry. Keeps arrow-key browsing from flooding the history while a deliberate click still lands its own position.
- **Or raise the cap** so a screenful of browsing does not exhaust it. Twenty came from the bead that asked for it, not from measurement.
- **Or accept the flood** — simplest, and defensible if back is expected to retrace every bead exactly as it was viewed.

Recommendation: coalesce. It is the only option that keeps both the reported behaviour and the reason the current rule was written.

Add: selecting bead A then B then C leaves back returning C→B→A; and whichever cost decision is taken above gets its own test (a coalesced run records one entry; or the cap still holds after a long run).

title: Hide and unhide columns in the beads list, remembered between restarts
description:
The list shows ten columns and no way to put any of them away. On a narrow window Title is squeezed by metrics some users never look at, and the choice cannot be expressed at all, let alone remembered.

Three things are wanted: **hide/unhide columns**, **a visible marker where columns are hidden that unhides them again**, and **preferences that survive a restart**. They differ sharply in cost, so they are separated below rather than estimated as one piece of work.

## Most of this is native on macOS 14, and should not be hand-rolled

`TableColumnCustomization` and `.customizationID(_:)` are macOS 14.0+, and this package targets `.macOS(.v14)`. Verified by type-checking against the macOS 14 SDK, including the `@AppStorage` form:

```swift
@AppStorage("issueListColumns")
private var columnCustomization: TableColumnCustomization<IssueRow>

Table(rows, selection: $store.selection,
      sortOrder: sortOrder,
      columnCustomization: $columnCustomization) {
    TableColumn("ID", value: \.id) { … }.customizationID("id")
    …
}
```

That single binding delivers:

- **a right-click context menu on the column header** listing every column with a checkmark — which is exactly the hiding mechanism asked for, so the "open to alternate suggestions" invitation resolves to "the platform already does it";
- **persistence across restarts** through `@AppStorage`, no bespoke defaults plumbing;
- column **reordering and resizing** for free.

Do this part first. It is roughly an afternoon, it is idiomatic, and it is what a macOS user expects a table header to do.

### Details that will bite

- **The glyph column has no header** (`IssueListView.swift:62`). In a customization menu it would appear as a blank row. Give it a real label ("Type") or opt it out with `.disabledCustomizationBehavior(.visibility)`.
- **ID should probably not be hideable.** A row with no identifier is hard to act on, and every context menu and bead link is keyed by it. Same treatment: `.disabledCustomizationBehavior(.visibility)`.
- **Hiding the column currently sorted by** needs a decided answer. `store.query.sort` is a single value driving the header chevron, the toolbar menu and bv's `s` cycle (`IssueListView.swift:21-38`), and none of those consult column visibility. Falling back to `.default` when the sort column is hidden is the honest behaviour; silently sorting by an invisible column is not.
- **`customizationID` strings are a persistence contract.** Once shipped they are in users' preferences; renaming one silently drops that column's saved state. Derive them from `SortColumn.rawValue` where a column has one, so the two cannot drift.
- `Tests/VBXUITests/ColumnHeaderSortTests.swift` contains `TableColumnOrderTests`, which pins declaration order by parsing this source file. Adding `.customizationID(…)` to each column leaves its `TableColumn("…"` prefix intact, so the parser still works — but check it, and note that user reordering is runtime state and deliberately not what that test measures.

## The accent divider is the expensive third, and may not be buildable as described

The request: where columns are hidden, the divider between the two adjacent visible columns becomes a thicker accent-coloured line, and double-clicking it unhides that adjacent group.

**SwiftUI's `Table` exposes no API for column dividers, and no way to read column frames.** There is no supported hook to thicken a specific divider, hit-test it, or know where it is on screen. So this cannot be added on top of the native table. The realistic options:

1. **Take the native affordance instead.** Hidden columns come back through the same header context menu that hid them. Cost: nothing. Loss: the spatial cue showing *where* something is hidden, which is the part of the request with real design value — it makes hidden state visible rather than remembered.
2. **A header-level indicator rather than a divider.** Keep the native table and mark hidden groups in a strip above or beside the header — a small accent chip reading "2 hidden" that reveals the group on click. Approximate, but expressible, and it keeps the "hidden state is visible" property.
3. **Replace `Table` with an `NSTableView` via `NSViewRepresentable`.** Full control of dividers, hit-testing and double-click. This is the only route to the request as literally written, and it is a large, risky rewrite: sorting, multi-selection, the context menu, time-travel badges, `RepoBadge`, actionable bolts and every snapshot test in `ViewSnapshotTests` all currently ride on the SwiftUI table. Not worth it for this feature alone; reconsider only if the list needs custom behaviour the native table cannot express for several reasons at once.

**Recommendation: ship option 1 with the native work above, then decide between 2 and 3 with the feature in hand.** Hiding without an indicator is genuinely useful on its own, and it is the part that can land quickly. Whether the missing spatial cue is actually a problem is much easier to judge once columns can be hidden at all.

## Tests

- Store round-trip: a `TableColumnCustomization` with columns hidden encodes and decodes through the `@AppStorage` key unchanged — that is the "remembered between restarts" claim, and it is the half that cannot be checked by looking at the screen.
- Sort interaction: hiding the sorted column leaves `store.query.sort` in a state the header can draw, per whatever answer the point above takes.
- Extend the list snapshot in `Tests/VBXUITests/ViewSnapshotTests.swift` with a customization that hides two columns, asserting ink coverage — per this repo's rule, `NSHostingView`, never `ImageRenderer`.
- The non-hideable columns stay non-hideable: an assertion that ID and the type glyph carry `disabledCustomizationBehavior`, so a later tidy-up cannot quietly make the identifier disappear.

title: Bead links show no pointer cursor, and the tooltip is dropped too
description:
Linked bead ids keep the I-beam pointer. The tint and underline landed in `vbx-tdk`, but the cursor never did — and the same investigation shows **the tooltip is broken too**, which nobody has reported because a tooltip that never appears looks like a tooltip that has nothing to say.

## Measured cause

`MarkdownText` sets three AppKit-scope attributes on each linked range. Hosting the real view and reading the backing AppKit string shows what survives the bridge:

| Attribute set in `linkBeadReferences` | Reaches AppKit? |
|---|---|
| `.link` | **yes** — `vbx://open?bead=vbx-8ou` at the id's range |
| `foregroundColor` | **yes** — accent blue on that range |
| `underlineStyle` | **yes** — `NSUnderline = 1` |
| `appKit.cursor` | **no** — absent |
| `appKit.toolTip` | **no** — absent |

So clicking works and the styling works; both *hover* affordances are dropped.

The renderer is the reason. With `.textSelection(.enabled)`, SwiftUI hosts the prose in a private **`SelectionTextField`** — a real `NSTextField` subclass inside a `PlatformViewRepresentableAdaptor<SelectionOverlay>` — and that bridge carries `.link`, colour and underline while discarding `.cursor` and `.toolTip`. A selectable text field also sets the I-beam itself, so even a surviving cursor attribute would likely lose to it.

`vbx-tdk` recorded that the attribute approach was unverifiable headlessly. It is verifiable — this is how — and the answer is that it does not work.

## Fixing it

`.pointerStyle(.link)` is macOS 15 and this package targets 14, so the route is an overlay, in the same shape as `HiddenColumnMarkers`: find the backing view, compute the geometry, add cursor rects. The pieces are all present:

- the `SelectionTextField` is reachable by walking the view hierarchy;
- its `attributedStringValue` still carries `.link` on exactly the id's range, so the ranges to decorate need no re-derivation — enumerate `.link` and use those ranges;
- a range's on-screen rect comes from laying the same attributed string out (`NSLayoutManager`, or `CTFramesetter` for a one-line field) against the field's bounds.

Then `addCursorRect(_:cursor:)` for the pointing hand and `addToolTipRect(_:owner:userData:)` for the title, both fixing the reported bug and the unreported one.

Carry over the two properties that made the marker overlay safe:

- **fail soft** — no field found means no cursor rects and prose that still renders;
- **let clicks through** — the overlay must not intercept, or it will break the link click it exists to advertise, plus text selection.

## Alternatives, if the overlay proves fragile

- **Render linked prose in an `NSTextView`** instead of `Text`. A read-only, selectable text view gives link cursor *and* tooltip natively, with no geometry maths. It is a bigger change: selection behaviour, layout and every markdown snapshot ride on the current renderer.
- **Drop `.textSelection(.enabled)`** for prose containing links. Cheapest, and almost certainly the wrong trade — being able to copy a description matters more than the pointer.

## Tests

Assert what the last attempt could not: host `MarkdownText` with a known bead id, find the backing field, and check that the computed cursor rect covers the `.link` range and nothing outside it. That is the assertion whose absence let `vbx-tdk` ship believing this worked. Keep the existing attribute-level tests — they still describe what the SwiftUI side sets — but they are no longer evidence that the user sees anything.

title: Toggle a label filter by double-clicking its pill
description:
Filtering by a label means going to the sidebar, while the label you want is right there in the row you are reading. Double-clicking a pill should add that label to the filter, and double-clicking a pill already filtered should remove it — the same gesture in both directions, so it reads as a toggle rather than two commands.

title: Edit a bead's priority from the list — the first write path
description:
Double-clicking a bead's priority in the list should open a small selector — P0 through P4 — and set the bead's priority to the choice.

**This is not a UI task. It is the first time vbx would write bead data,** and that is the whole of the difficulty. The picker is an afternoon; everything below is the reason this bead is not.

## vbx has no write path today

Confirmed against the tree: the app writes only *sidecar* files — recipes, baselines, correlation feedback. `BeadsEngine` exposes `saveRecipe` and `saveBaseline` and nothing that touches a bead record, and no code anywhere runs an external process. Priority editing would be the first mutation of the data itself.

## It must go through `br`, not through the JSONL

`.beads/issues.jsonl` is a **whole-file export** of `.beads/beads.db`. The database is gitignored, so there is one per checkout and every worktree carries its own. A flush from a database that predates someone else's changes rewrites the entire file and drops them — and because git sees a rewrite rather than overlapping hunks, there is **no conflict and no error**. Last flush wins, silently.

An app that serialises its in-memory bead set back to that file is exactly that stale flush, in a GUI, one double-click away. The failure is invisible at the moment it happens and surfaces later as beads that vanished.

So the mutation is `br update <id> --priority <n> --json`, and the sequence is:

```
1. refresh      → the on-disk JSONL is current before touching it
2. br update    → br owns the DB and the export
3. verify       → the issues.jsonl diff is a line, never a rewrite
4. reload       → the engine re-reads; the UI follows the file, not its own cache
```

## What follows from that

- **`br` becomes a runtime dependency.** It is a Rust binary the user installs; the app cannot assume it. First-run detection with a clear install path, and priority editing disabled with a stated reason when it is absent — not a mysterious failure on the first double-click.
- **Undo is an inverse command, not a memory rollback.** Since `br` owns the state, undoing a priority change means issuing the change back. Design the edit surface around that from the start; retrofitting it is painful.
- **The watcher is load-bearing.** `FileWatchService` and `reload(force:)` already keep the view stable while the file changes underneath, which is exactly what an editor needs — and is why `vbx-ozd` deliberately left `reload` out of the filter reset.
- **Time travel must refuse it.** Editing a bead while the list shows a past revision would write today's data from a view of last week's. Disable the affordance, or make it act on the current revision and say so.

## Decide the product question before the technical one

Editing was named as the paid differentiator in the Visual Beads Pro plan. If priority editing lands in the open app, the free edition becomes an editor and Pro's pitch has to move to depth — bulk operations, dependency editing, templates — rather than "editing at all".

That is a business call, not an engineering one, and it is worth making deliberately rather than discovering after this ships. A narrower option, if the answer is unclear: build the `br` command layer now (it is needed either way) and gate the *surface* behind a flag.

## Tests

The command layer is where the value is: assert the exact argument vector for a priority change, that a failure surfaces as an error rather than a silent no-op, and that the absent-`br` path disables editing rather than throwing. Then a store-level test that a successful edit is followed by a reload, so the UI cannot drift from the file. The picker itself needs a hosted-view test only for "double-click opens it and does not break row selection".

title: One window per workspace: several .beads open side by side
description:
Today vbx shows one workspace at a time. Opening another replaces the one on
screen. Comparing two repositories, or keeping a reference workspace open
beside the one being worked on, is not possible. It should be: **File ▸ New
Window** opens an independent window with its own workspace, its own view,
filters, selection and history.

## Why this is not a `WindowGroup` tweak

`VBXApp.swift:10` holds

```swift
@StateObject private var store = ProjectStore()
```

on the `App`, and injects that one instance into every scene
(`:15`). `WindowGroup` already makes multiple windows — ⌘N works — but they
all render the same store, so two windows are two views of one workspace, and
opening a folder in either changes both. **The store's lifetime has to move
from the app to the scene**, which is the whole of the work; the window
plumbing is already there.

`ProjectStore` is documented as "Observable application state for one
workspace" (`ProjectStore.swift:86`) and holds no static or shared state, so
it is already shaped for one-per-window. That is the good news.

## What has to be resolved

- **The scene's identity is the workspace path.** `WindowGroup(for: String.self)`
  keyed on the path gives free state restoration and makes "open this
  workspace" idempotent — reopening a path raises its existing window instead
  of making a second one. The tutorial scene (`:43`) already uses that shape.
  Decide whether a second window on the *same* workspace is allowed at all.
- **`openInitialWorkspace()`** (`ProjectStore.swift:475`, called from
  `.task` at `:19`) currently means "the app's workspace". With per-window
  stores it becomes "this window's workspace", and the launch case — one
  window, restored or last-used — needs stating explicitly.
- **`vbx://open?workspace=…&bead=…`** (`:22`) and Spotlight
  (`:27`) both deliver into *the* store today. They must route to the window
  already showing that workspace, or open a new one — not hijack whichever
  window happens to be frontmost.
- **The menu bar is app-wide, the commands are not.** `VBXCommands`
  (`:59`) takes `store:` by `@ObservedObject`. Every command in it — filters,
  sort, export, surface switching — has to act on the *key window's* store,
  via `@FocusedValue`, not on a captured one. This is the subtlest part and
  the easiest to get half-right: a menu item that silently acts on the wrong
  window is worse than one that is disabled.
- **What stays shared, and what does not.** `RecentWorkspaces` (per-window
  `store.recents` today, backed by one `UserDefaults` key) is genuinely
  app-wide and should be a single instance every window reads. So is the
  tutorial's seen-state and the column customization
  (`@AppStorage("issueListColumnCustomization")`, `IssueListView.swift:26`) —
  though that last one is worth a deliberate decision rather than inheriting
  the global by default. Anything holding a file watcher, engine handle or
  Spotlight indexer is per-workspace and must be torn down when its window
  closes; a leaked `FileWatchService` per closed window is the predictable
  failure.
- **The title must disambiguate.** `.navigationTitle(store.info?.displayName ?? "vbx")`
  (`ContentView.swift:58`) already names the workspace, which is most of it.
  Two windows on repositories with the same folder name want the parent path
  as a subtitle.

## Scope note

This is a structural change touching app entry, the command tree and every
service the store owns. It is worth doing before more state accumulates on the
app-level store, not after — each new app-scoped value added between now and
then is another thing to move.

## Test

Two stores, two workspaces, no bleed: assert that opening a workspace in one
store leaves a second store's issues, filters and selection untouched, and
that closing a window releases its watcher. The cross-window menu routing
wants a test of its own — commands must reach the focused store, and no other.

title: An About window showing the licences vbx is obliged to ship
description:
vbx ships the default macOS About panel — name, version, and nothing else. It links a Go engine built from 66 third-party modules, several of which **require their notices to be distributed with the binary**, and one of which requires its licence rider carried unmodified. None of that reaches the user today.

An About window should name the app and show the licences that apply, and the list must be **generated rather than hand-maintained**, or it drifts the first time a dependency changes.

## What has to appear, and why

From the dependency audit (ADR-011 records the summary; the superseded Pro plan has the full table):

| Component | Obligation |
|---|---|
| 33 MIT, 22 BSD-3 modules | Copyright and permission notice in the distribution |
| 7 Apache-2.0 modules | Notice, plus any bundled `NOTICE` file |
| `golang/freetype` | Dual **FreeType Licence or GPLv2** — vbx takes the FTL arm, which wants a credit. Say which arm was chosen, or a later reader will assume the GPL one applies |
| `cyphar/filepath-securejoin` | BSD-3 **+ MPL-2.0**. MPL is per-file copyleft: unmodified files stay under MPL and their source must be offered — a URL to upstream satisfies it |
| `ajstarks/svgo` | **CC-BY-4.0** — attribution required |
| `mattn/go-localereader` | States MIT in its README with **no LICENSE file**. Pin the commit and keep a copy of that README, or there is nothing to show |
| **`beads_viewer` (bv)** | MIT **plus a rider that must be included unmodified in any distribution**. This is the one that is not merely polite: the rider says so explicitly, and breach terminates the licence to the engine vbx is built on |
| vbx itself | MIT with the AI Training Rider — the app should state its own terms too |

There are **no external Swift package dependencies** (`Package.swift` declares none), so the Go module graph plus vbx's own licence is the whole set.

## Generate it, with a `--check` mode

Follow `build-icon.sh`: a script produces the artefact, the artefact is committed, and `--check` proves the two still agree. That is already the repo's answer to generated-but-committed files, and the verify block runs it.

- `scripts/build-notices.py` reads `Engine/bridge/go.mod`, resolves each module in the Go module cache, extracts its licence text, and writes `Resources/Acknowledgements.rtf` (or Markdown, if the About window renders it with `MarkdownText`).
- The file is **committed**, for the same reason as the icon: a fresh clone must be able to build a shippable app without a populated module cache.
- `--check` re-derives and diffs, so a dependency bump that changes the notices fails the verify block instead of shipping a stale file. Add it to the list in `CLAUDE.md`.
- Handle the two awkward cases explicitly rather than silently: a module with **no licence file** (`go-localereader`) and one with **several** (`filepath-securejoin` has `COPYING.md`, `LICENSE.BSD` and `LICENSE.MPL-2.0`). A generator that takes the first file it finds gets the second case wrong.

## The window

`CommandGroup(replacing: .appInfo)` opens a real window rather than
`orderFrontStandardAboutPanel`, because the panel's credits field is a poor
place for several thousand lines of licence text.

- App name, version and build from the bundle — not literals, or they go stale against `build-app.sh`.
- A short "vbx is MIT with the AI Training Rider" line, then the third-party notices in a scrolling region.
- It is one window for the app, not one per workspace: it names the *app*. With per-window stores now in place (ADR: one window per workspace), make it a `Window` scene rather than something a `WorkspaceWindow` owns.

## Tests

- The generator's `--check` mode is the real test, and it belongs in the verify block.
- Assert the notices file **contains bv's rider text**, since that is the obligation with teeth. A substring check against the rider's opening line is enough to catch a regeneration that dropped it.
- Assert every module in `go.mod` appears by name, so a new dependency cannot slip in unnoticed.
- Snapshot the About window with `NSHostingView` and assert ink coverage, per this repo's rule.
close_reason: Implemented on worktree-about-licences

title: Launch should reopen the last workspace, and never open with an error
description:
Launching vbx from the Dock or Finder shows **"Could not open workspace"** with an error triangle, every time, before the user has asked for anything.

The neutral state the launch should land in already exists a few lines below it in `ContentView.swift:27` — "No workspace open", with a **Choose Workspace…** button. The bug is that launch reaches the *error* state instead.

## Why it always fails

`openInitialWorkspace()` (`ProjectStore.swift:483`) tries, in order:

1. a path in `CommandLine.arguments`,
2. `VBX_WORKSPACE`,
3. **`FileManager.default.currentDirectoryPath`**.

A GUI app launched from Finder or the Dock has a current directory of `/`. That holds no `.beads`, so `open(path:)` fails, sets `loadError`, and the error state wins. The fallback only works when the app is launched from a terminal sitting in a workspace — which is how it has been tested.

It also never consults the recents list, even though `RecentWorkspaces.shared` now holds exactly "the last workspace opened".

## The distinction to restore

**"Nothing to open yet" is not "what you asked for failed."** This repo has made that distinction before — 98e3abf separated "nothing to scan for" from "no config at all", and the engine reports `history_status` so an absent staleness signal cannot be read as a low one. The same rule applies here: `loadError` should mean *the user pointed at something and it did not work*, and launch discovery should never set it.

## The change

Candidate order, with the recents list added:

1. a path argument,
2. `VBX_WORKSPACE`,
3. the most recent workspace (`RecentWorkspaces.shared.entries.first`),
4. the current directory — but only when it actually holds bead data.

**Probe each candidate rather than attempting to open it.** `BeadsEngine.probe` answers "would this open?" without loading, which is what `OpenPanelGuard` already uses to grey rows in the Open panel. Probing means a dead candidate is *skipped* rather than producing an error, and the same discovery rules apply as everywhere else.

If no candidate probes openable, open nothing and leave `loadError` nil. The existing empty state then appears on its own, offering the Choose Workspace… button the request asks for — no new UI needed.

## Two neighbouring cases

- **A restored window whose workspace has since moved.** Windows are keyed on the workspace path now (`WorkspaceWindow`), so a restored window calls `open(path:)` directly rather than going through discovery. A path that no longer opens should fall through to the neutral state too — being told a folder you did not choose this session has vanished is the same unhelpful error, one launch later.
- **`openInitialWorkspace()` is only called for a window with no stored path.** Worth stating so this is not implemented twice.

## Do not over-correct

The error state is right for a workspace the user explicitly chose that failed — a folder picked in the Open panel, a bad `vbx://` link, a recents entry clicked by hand. Those must keep reporting, with the reason. Only *discovery* falls silent.

## Tests

In `ProjectStoreTests`:

- launch with no argument, a current directory that is not a workspace and an empty recents list → **no `loadError`**, nothing loaded, so the neutral empty state shows;
- with a recent recorded → that workspace opens;
- a path argument beats the recents list;
- a recent that no longer opens is skipped in favour of the next candidate;
- **and the guard against over-correcting**: `open(path:)` on a folder holding no beads still sets `loadError`. Without that one, a fix here could quietly make every failure silent.
close_reason: Landed in PR #33 (branch worktree-close-open-beads): launch probes candidates and falls silent when there is nothing to discover; distribution builds are universal and the slices are asserted with lipo. 440 Swift tests, 117 packaging tests.

title: Recipes never load, so the sidebar section is always empty
description:
The sidebar's Recipes section is empty in a running app. It offers "New recipe…" and nothing to click, so the feature appears to do nothing — while the engine has had eleven recipes available the whole time.

## Measured

Driving the store directly:

```
before open: isLoaded=false  recipes=0
after open:  isLoaded=true   recipes=0   ← should be 11
after an explicit loadRecipes(): recipes=11
```

`vbx-cli --robot-recipes` lists all eleven built-ins for the same workspace — `actionable`, `blocked`, `bottlenecks`, `closed`, `default`, `high-impact`, `quick-wins`, `recent`, `release-cut`, `stale`, `triage` — so nothing is wrong below the store.

## Cause

`loadRecipes()` (`ProjectStore.swift:733`) guards on `isLoaded`, and it is called from exactly three places: the sidebar section's `.task` (`RecipesSection.swift:48`), `saveRecipe` and `deleteRecipe`.

**Nothing calls it when a workspace opens.** The sidebar renders immediately at launch, before any workspace has loaded, so its `.task` fires while `isLoaded` is still false and returns early — and `.task` does not re-run when the value it depended on changes. The one call that would populate the list runs at the only moment it cannot work.

## Fix

Load the recipes as part of a successful open, beside the other refreshes, rather than from a view that can appear too early:

- in `open(path:)`, after `refreshAll()`;
- in `reload(force:)` on the changed path too — recipes live in the workspace, so a workspace edited on disk can gain or lose one.

Then drop the `.task` from `SidebarRecipesSection`. Leaving both would be two mechanisms for one job, and the view-driven one is the half that cannot be relied on.

## Test

The assertion whose absence let this ship: **after `open(path:)`, `store.recipes` is not empty.** Add the reload case as well, and keep one that a recipe can still be applied afterwards, so a fix here cannot regress into loading a list that does not work.

This is also worth checking against the launch bug in `[[vbx-jo9]]`: with no workspace open at launch, the section is legitimately empty, and the two failures look identical from the outside.
close_reason: Fixed on worktree-recipes-never-load

title: Version releases from git, and generate the release notes
description:
Every build vbx has ever produced claims to be **version 0.1.0, build 1**. The
two values are hardcoded in the plist heredoc at `scripts/build-app.sh:98-99`,
and nothing bumps them. `AboutView.swift:73-74` reads
`CFBundleShortVersionString` and `CFBundleVersion` straight out of that plist,
so the About window shipped in #27 shows `0.1.0 (1)` to every user of every
build, and `scripts/package-app.sh:327` reads the same key back out to name the
packaged artifact. There are **no git tags** in the repository.

So today there is no way to answer "which build is this?" — not from the About
window, not from a DMG filename, not from `git`.

## What this asks for

1. A version managed **in git**, not hand-edited in a shell script.
2. MAJOR / MINOR / PATCH advancing **on merge to `main`**.
3. Release notes **generated**, not written by hand.
4. Those notes grouped as features and bug fixes, **newest release first**.
5. Published **as markdown**.

## The constraint that decides the design

The obvious implementation reads Conventional Commits (`feat:` → minor, `fix:` →
patch) off the merge commit. **That does not work here.** This repo's subjects
are deliberately prose:

```
Hand the priority cell its store, so scrolling the list cannot crash (#29)
Load recipes when a workspace opens (#30)
Show the licences vbx is obliged to ship, in an About window (#27)
```

A `feat:`/`fix:` parser would classify every one of them as "no bump". So the
bump signal has to come from somewhere other than the subject prefix, and the
choice is the substance of this bead rather than an implementation detail:

- **A PR label** (`semver:major` / `semver:minor` / `semver:patch`). Every change
  here lands as a squash-merged PR — every subject above ends in `(#N)` — so the
  PR is a reliable handle, and the label is set while the change is being
  reviewed, when the person setting it knows what it is.
- **A commit trailer** (`Semver: minor`). Survives outside GitHub, but has to be
  remembered at commit time and cannot be corrected after the fact.
- **Adopting Conventional Commits.** Cheapest to automate, but it overwrites a
  house style the log has held for 30 commits, and CLAUDE.md's own guidance is
  that a subject should say what changed and why.

The first is recommended: it fits how work actually lands here and needs no
change to the commit style. **A missing label must be an explicit default
(patch), not a silent one** — the script should say which rule fired.

While the version is `0.x`, a breaking change bumps MINOR, not MAJOR; MAJOR
waits for 1.0.0.

## One source of truth

The generated version has to reach the plist rather than sit beside it.
`build-app.sh` should read it (from the tag, or a generated file) instead of
carrying the literal `0.1.0`, so About, the packaged artifact name and the git
tag cannot disagree. `CFBundleVersion` — the build number — should advance
monotonically and independently of the marketing version.

## The release notes document

`scripts/build-docs.py:389` globs `docs/*.md`, so a `docs/RELEASES.md` gets its
HTML rendering for free and needs no change to the docs build. Per CLAUDE.md it
also needs a row in the document index in the same PR that adds it.

It must not become a fourth copy of what the repo already records. The existing
notes are engineering-facing and stay that way:

- `docs/project_notes/BUGS.md` — a bug and the regression test locking it in.
- `docs/project_notes/WORK_LOG.md` — dated work, newest first.

`RELEASES.md` is the **user-facing** view: per released version, what changed for
someone using the app, newest release first. The natural input is the set of
squash-merged PR subjects between two tags — they are already written as
readable sentences, which is exactly what makes the prose style worth keeping.

## Acceptance

- Merging to `main` produces a new version and a `vX.Y.Z` tag without anyone
  editing a version by hand.
- The About window, the packaged artifact name and the tag agree.
- `docs/RELEASES.md` lists releases newest-first, grouped into features and
  fixes, and is regenerated rather than edited.
- A `--check` mode that verifies the committed notes and version match what
  would be generated, so it can join the verify block in CLAUDE.md — every other
  script here (`build-engine.sh`, `build-icon.sh`, `build-notices.py`) has one.
- Re-running the bump on an already-released commit is a no-op, so it cannot
  double-bump.

## Prior art

`of1` solves the same problem with `scripts/version-bump.sh` — conventional
commits, a `semver:*` PR label as an override, and a
`chore(release): vX.Y.Z` commit plus tag pushed to `main` from a throwaway
worktree, idempotent on a `chore(release)` HEAD. Worth reading before starting;
the label-override half is directly reusable, the commit-prefix half is the part
that does not transfer.
close_reason: Landed in PR #33: scripts/version-bump.sh takes the level from a semver:* PR label (default patch, announced), records it in the annotated tag, and scripts/release-notes.py generates docs/RELEASES.md from the tags offline. .github/workflows/release.yml runs it on merge, idempotently. The semver:* labels still need creating on GitHub.

title: Ship a universal binary, not arm64 only
description:
vbx builds for the host architecture only. On an Apple-silicon machine that means an arm64-only app, which will not run on an Intel Mac at all — measured on the current build:

```
$ lipo -archs .build/vbx.app/Contents/MacOS/vbx
arm64
```

## Half of this already exists

`scripts/build-engine.sh --universal` already builds arm64 + x86_64 and `lipo`s them into one archive. It is the Swift side and the packaging that never ask for it:

- `build-app.sh:53-54` runs plain `swift build -c release --product vbx`, so both binaries come out host-only;
- nothing passes `--universal` to `build-engine.sh`, so even a universal Swift build would fail to link the second slice.

## The change

- **`swift build --arch arm64 --arch x86_64`** produces a fat binary in one invocation. Both products need it — `vbx` *and* `vbx-cli`, since the CLI is bundled and installed onto the user's PATH.
- **`build-app.sh` gains a `--universal` flag** that forwards to `build-engine.sh --universal` and adds the `--arch` pair. Distribution builds should imply it: shipping a `.dmg` that silently excludes half the Macs is the kind of mistake that reaches a user, exactly as `--dmg` already implies `--release`.
- **Verify the output rather than trusting the flags.** `lipo -archs` on both binaries in the bundle, asserting both slices are present, belongs beside the existing `assert_archive_target` check — that function already exists because "the flag was passed" and "the flag took effect" are different claims.

## What to watch

- **Cross-compiling cgo.** The engine is `-buildmode=c-archive` with `CGO_ENABLED=1`, so building the x86_64 slice on Apple silicon needs the right `CC` target flags. `--universal` already exists, so this presumably works — but it has not been exercised in a while, and it is the step most likely to be broken.
- **The deployment-target assertion has to cover both slices.** `assert_archive_target` reads `otool -l | awk '/minos/'`; on a fat archive it must confirm 14.0 for *each* architecture rather than passing because one of them is right.
- **Build time roughly doubles**, and the engine archive is already 51 MB per slice. Worth keeping the plain host build as the default for development, with universal reserved for distribution.
- **Rosetta is not an answer.** An arm64-only app does not run under Rosetta; Rosetta translates x86_64 to arm64, not the reverse.

## Tests

`build-engine.sh --check` and a new `lipo -archs` assertion in the packaging path are the real checks — this is build plumbing, so the verification belongs in the scripts rather than in `swift test`. Add the universal check to the verify block in `CLAUDE.md` only if it is cheap enough to run every time; if it doubles the build, gate it behind the flag and state that in the script's header.
close_reason: Landed in PR #33 (branch worktree-close-open-beads): launch probes candidates and falls silent when there is nothing to discover; distribution builds are universal and the slices are asserted with lipo. 440 Swift tests, 117 packaging tests.

title: Install via a Homebrew cask
description:
`brew install --cask vbx` should install Visual Beads. Today the only route is cloning the repo and running `build-app.sh`, which needs a Go toolchain and a Swift toolchain.

Most of the hard part is done: `package-app.sh --dmg` already produces a Developer ID–signed, notarized, stapled `.dmg`, and ADR-009/010 cover the signing arrangement. What is missing is everything between that file and a user's `brew` command.

## Prerequisites, in the order they block

1. **A real release.** A cask points at a versioned URL with a `sha256`. There are no tagged releases and no published artefacts — `.dmg` files exist only on the machine that built them.
2. **A version that is not hardcoded.** `CFBundleShortVersionString` is the literal `0.1.0` in `build-app.sh:98`. A cask's `version` must match what the app reports, or `brew upgrade` cannot tell versions apart and `brew info` disagrees with the About window. Derive it from the git tag, and have `build-app.sh` stamp it.
3. **Notarization must actually have run.** A cask installing an un-notarized app gives every user a Gatekeeper block. `--dmg` supports `--no-notarize` for local builds; the release path must not use it, and should fail rather than warn if stapling did not happen.
4. **Universal, ideally.** A cask serving an arm64-only app to an Intel Mac installs something that cannot launch. See the universal-binary bead; either ship universal, or the cask needs an `arm: sha256: ...` / `intel: sha256: ...` split with two artefacts.

## Where the cask lives

**Not `homebrew/homebrew-cask`, at least not first.** Its acceptance criteria require software with a track record — a notable user base, stable versioning, a maintained upstream. A newly published app is normally rejected, and submitting early costs a review cycle for a predictable no.

**A personal tap is the realistic route:** a `homebrew-tap` repository under the same account, so the command is

```
brew tap michel-onstein/tap
brew install --cask vbx
```

The cask file itself is short — `version`, `sha256`, `url` pointing at the release asset, `name`, `desc`, `homepage`, an `app "Visual Beads.app"` stanza, and a `zap` stanza listing what to remove on `--zap`.

## Two details that are easy to get wrong

- **`zap` has to list the real preference domains.** vbx writes `com.qjam.vbx` defaults — including the column layout (`issueListColumnCustomization`) and the recents list — plus anything in the keychain from the deploy-credentials settings. A cask that leaves those behind is a cask that cannot be cleanly uninstalled.
- **`livecheck` should track the GitHub releases feed**, so Homebrew's own auditing notices new versions. Without it the cask goes stale silently.

## Suggested shape

- `scripts/release.sh` — tag, build universal, package, notarize, staple, compute the `sha256`, and print the cask stanza ready to paste. Generating it beats hand-editing the version and hash in two places.
- The cask in a separate tap repository, since Homebrew requires the repo to be named `homebrew-tap`.
- A line in the README showing the two `brew` commands, which is what most people will actually look for.

## Check

The one that matters cannot be run locally: `brew install --cask` from a clean machine, confirming the app launches without a Gatekeeper prompt. `brew audit --cask` and `brew style` catch the mechanical problems first, and `--dry-run` on the release script proves the plan before a tag is pushed — the existing `package-app.sh --dry-run` sets that precedent.
close_reason: In-repo pipeline complete and landed in PR #33: scripts/version.sh (version from the tag), scripts/release.sh (tag -> universal -> notarize -> verify stapled -> checksum -> render cask; --lint-cask runs brew style without a build), packaging/homebrew/vbx.rb.template (brew style clean; the first run caught 4 real offences), README brew section, ADR-012. Also fixed scripts/signing.env, dead since the bvx->vbx rename in #13 — with that repaired, --check reports the Developer ID cert present. NOT DONE, and not doable from the repo: brew install --cask vbx does not work. Three credential-gated user actions remain: (1) xcrun notarytool store-credentials <profile> — no notarytool credential exists in the keychain at all; (2) create michel-onstein/homebrew-tap; (3) merge #33, then ./scripts/release.sh --tag vX.Y.Z --publish and paste .build/dist/vbx.rb into the tap. Docs state plainly that brew install does not work yet. Reopen or file a new bead if the publishing itself should be tracked.

title: Align hosted cell content to the leading edge, not the centre
description:
Label pills sit in the middle of the Labels column instead of against its leading edge.

## It is not only the labels

Reported for the pills, but **every hosted cell is centred**: ID, P, the type glyph, the status chip, Blocks, Blocked by and PageRank all sit in the middle of their columns. Only Title is left-aligned, and only because it is the one column drawn natively as an `NSTextField` rather than hosted.

That makes this one fix rather than ten.

## Cause

Introduced by [ADR-014](../docs/project_notes/DECISIONS.md), the move to `NSTableView`. `HostedCell` in `Sources/VBXUI/BeadTable.swift` pins its `NSHostingView` to both the leading *and* trailing edges:

```swift
hosting.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: leadingAnchor, constant: 4),
hosting.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: trailingAnchor, constant: -4),
hosting.centerYAnchor.constraint(equalTo: centerYAnchor),
```

So the SwiftUI content is handed the full column width, and a view given more width than it needs centres itself in it. SwiftUI's `Table` left-aligned cell content by default, which is why this was right before and is wrong now.

## The change

Give hosted content a leading alignment — `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)` applied where the cell hosts it, so no individual column has to remember.

**Numeric columns are a judgement call.** Blocks, Blocked by and PageRank are `.monospacedDigit()` counts and scores; macOS tables usually right-align those so the digits line up. Left-aligning everything is the smaller change and matches what the SwiftUI table did; right-aligning the numbers is arguably better and is a separate decision. Pick one deliberately rather than by default, and say which in the commit.

If alignment becomes per-column, it belongs on `BeadColumnSpec` next to `width` — that is the file where a column is declared once.

## Tests

Alignment is exactly the kind of thing a snapshot flatters, so assert geometry rather than ink: host the list, take a hosted cell's `NSHostingView`, and check its content starts at the leading edge rather than being inset by half the slack. `HiddenColumnMarkerTests` already has a harness that hosts the real table and reaches its `NSTableView`; reuse it.

One case per shape is enough — a text cell and the labels cell — plus the guard that Title, which is not hosted, is unaffected.

ADR-015.

title: Add a combined Blocked/by column alongside the two it summarises
description:
Add a column combining Blocks and Blocked by into one, formatted `<blocks> / <blocked by>` — for example `7 / 1`.

**All three columns exist afterwards.** The two single-value columns stay; this is a third, so someone who wants one dense column can hide the other two, and someone who wants to sort by each separately still can. The header show/hide menu already makes that a two-click choice.

## Where it goes

`IssueListView.specs` in `Sources/VBXUI/IssueListView.swift`. A column is declared once now — id, title, sort, widths, editor — so this is one entry plus a case in the cell-content switch.

Suggested id `blockedRatio`, title `Blocked/by`, width around 74pt.

## Two decisions to make, not assume

**What it sorts by.** `BeadColumnSpec.sort` is a `SortColumn`, and every sortable column's identifier must equal its `SortColumn` raw value — asserted in `Table columns`, because otherwise the header chevron and the actual order come apart. So a sortable combined column needs a new `SortColumn` case (and an arm in `SortMode.ordering(by:)`), and something has to define what that order *is*: by blocks, by blocked-by, or by the two summed. None is obviously right.

The cheapest honest answer is to ship it **unsortable** — `sort: nil`, like the type glyph — and let the existing two columns carry sorting. That needs no new enum case and no invented ordering. Add a `SortColumn` case later if someone actually wants to sort by it.

**How zero reads.** The existing columns render `0` as `—`, greyed. The combined form has to say something for `0 / 0`. `— / —` is consistent but noisy at a glance; `0 / 0` is honest but louder than the columns it replaces. Worth looking at both against a real workspace before choosing — `Fixtures/demo` has rows covering `7 / 1`, `— / 2`, `1 / 1` and `— / —`.

## Tests

The formatting, directly: a row with blocks and blocked-by produces the expected string, including whichever zero form is chosen. Plus the invariants the specs list already carries — the new column has a unique identifier, a sane width range, and (if left unsortable) is absent from the sortable set. Those are ordinary assertions now that columns are a value.

Worth one snapshot too, since the point of the column is that it reads well in one glance.
