title: Show which beads are uncommitted, against git HEAD
description:
A bead edited from vbx is written to disk immediately — `br` updates `.beads/beads.db` and re-exports `.beads/issues.jsonl` — but nothing commits it. Nothing on screen says which beads are ahead of the last commit, so after a few edits there is no way to see what a commit would contain except by reading a diff.

Mark those rows with a subtly different row background.

## What "dirty" means

**A bead whose record in the working `.beads/issues.jsonl` differs from the record in that file at `HEAD`.** That is the definition that aligns with git, which is what the request asks for, and it needs no state of vbx's own — no side file to fall out of step, nothing to rebuild after an external `br` run or a `git checkout`.

Three cases, and they are not the same:

- **Changed** — the id exists in both and the records differ.
- **Added** — in the working file, absent at `HEAD`. Also dirty; a brand-new bead is the most likely thing to forget to commit.
- **Removed** — at `HEAD`, gone from the working file. There is no row to tint. Out of scope for the background, but worth knowing it exists rather than discovering it later.

## Reading HEAD

[ADR-006](../docs/project_notes/DECISIONS.md) already has the machinery: correlation reads the git object store **directly** rather than shelling out to `git`, which is what makes it work sandboxed. The blob for `.beads/issues.jsonl` at `HEAD` is the same kind of read, and it should go the same way rather than adding a `git` subprocess beside it.

**Compare parsed records, not bytes.** The export is whole-file and `br` rewrites it — key order and formatting can change without any bead changing. Comparing decoded records keeps a reformat from lighting up every row. Worth deciding whether `updated_at` alone counts as a change: `br` touches it on every write, so it will differ whenever anything else does, but a record where it is the *only* difference is a bead that was written and not actually changed.

## Multi-repo

A workspace can span repositories, each with its own `.beads` and its own git. Dirtiness is per repository, and a workspace root that is not itself a git repository has no `HEAD` to compare against. `store.repo(of:)` already knows which repository a bead came from.

## Staying current

The file is already watched — live reload is FSEvents-driven, debounced and hash-gated — so a recompute can hang off the same signal. What that misses is `HEAD` moving underneath: a commit made in a terminal makes every dirty bead clean without touching the JSONL. Watching `.git/HEAD` and `.git/index` covers it. Cheap either way: this is one blob read and a dictionary comparison, not a graph walk.

**No metric is computed in Swift** is the rule, but this is not a metric — it is a property of the checkout, not of the graph, and the engine has no opinion about it.

## The background

Now that the list is an `NSTableView` ([ADR-014](../docs/project_notes/DECISIONS.md)) this is `tableView(_:rowViewForRow:)` returning an `NSTableRowView` that draws its own background — the supported way, and it composes with `usesAlternatingRowBackgroundColors` and with selection rather than fighting them.

Subtle is the whole point: it has to survive the alternating stripe underneath it, stay legible in both appearances, and not read as an error. A very low-alpha accent tint is the usual answer. **Colour alone is not an affordance** — the repo has an accessibility audit bead open — so the row needs a tooltip or an inspector line saying "modified since the last commit", and the status bar showing a count of dirty beads would make the state visible without hunting for tinted rows.

## Not in scope

Committing from vbx. This is about *seeing* the state. A commit affordance is a much larger question — what message, which files, whose identity — and should be decided on its own.

## Tests

The comparison is pure and is where the substance is: given two record sets, the right ids come back changed, added and removed. Then, against a real workspace: a bead written through `br` becomes dirty, and one nobody touched does not.

`Fixture.writableStore()` copies the fixture to a temp directory, but the copy is not a git repository — this needs a fixture that is one, with a commit, so `HEAD` exists to compare against. That is new harness and probably the largest single piece of the work.

For the row background, assert the row view's colour differs for a dirty row and matches for a clean one; do not assert an exact colour, which is a design choice that will change.
close_reason: Implemented and released in 0.0.9 (PR #42). vbx-00c: HostedCell aligns hosted content leading, one fix covering every hosted column; regression test measures leftmost ink and was confirmed to fail at 27% before. vbx-06t: combined Blocked/by column beside its two sources, unsortable by design, zero renders as an em dash. vbx-bct: BeadDirtyState compares the working bead set against snapshot_at HEAD, .git watched alongside the export, unknown distinguished from clean, row tint plus tooltip plus status-bar count. ADR-015.

title: Hide the filter and sort controls on the views that ignore them
description:
The toolbar's Filter picker and Sort menu are declared unconditionally in
`ContentView.toolbarContent`, so they are present on every surface. Seven of
them never read either one: **Attention, Sprint, Alerts, Flow (cross-label
flow), Labels, Plan and Insights** render engine payloads of their own and
never touch `store.visibleIssues`, which is the only place `query.filter` and
`query.sort` are applied. Changing either control on those views does nothing
visible, so the toolbar advertises a knob that is not connected.

Hide both items on those surfaces rather than disabling them: a disabled
control still claims the view has an ordering that is merely unavailable, and
these views have no bead ordering at all.

The four surfaces that do consume `visibleIssues` — List, Board, Graph and
Tree — keep both controls unchanged. **History is not in scope here**; it does
not consume `visibleIssues` either, but it was not named in the request and its
relationship to the revision scrubber wants deciding on its own.
notes:
Suggested shape: a computed property on `ViewSurface` (`Sources/VBXAppCore/ProjectStore.swift`, beside `displayName` and `symbolName`) answering whether the surface orders beads, so the answer lives next to the enum and a new case has to state it. Gate the two `ToolbarItem`s in `Sources/VBXUI/ContentView.swift` on `store.surface`.

Two things to watch:

- `LabelsView.swift:167` assigns `store.query.filter = .all` when drilling into a label. That write must survive — it is setting up the destination view, not driving the hidden control.
- `GraphView.swift:185` keys its layout cache on `query.filter`, and Graph keeps its controls, so nothing changes there.

Test: assert the property against the set of surfaces that read `visibleIssues`, so a new view added without a decision fails rather than silently inheriting the wrong answer.
close_reason: Hidden on the seven surfaces that never read the query; regression test asserts the mapping

title: Decide whether History gets a meaningful filter and sort, or loses both
description:
`vbx-qap` hid the toolbar's Filter picker and Sort menu on the seven surfaces
that never read `query`. **History was left showing them**, and it should not
have been left there permanently — it reads `store.history` and nothing else,
so the two controls are as inert there as they were on Attention or Plan.

It was held back because History is the one surface where the question is not
purely "does it read `visibleIssues`". It sits beside the revision scrubber,
and there is a real design question underneath: should History gain a filter
and sort that mean something in its own terms — narrowing the commit walk, or
ordering the correlated beads — or should it simply drop both controls like the
other seven?

Decide that, then either implement the meaning or set
`ViewSurface.showsFilterAndSort` to `false` for `.history`.

Whichever way it goes, `Tests/VBXUITests/ToolbarControlsTests.swift` has to move
with it: `.history` currently sits in a `deferred` set that exists only to
record this open question, and that set should be empty afterwards.
close_reason: Decided and implemented in 0.0.10 (PR #43). History reads store.history and consults neither query nor visibleIssues, so both controls were inert there exactly as on the other seven surfaces; dropped rather than given a bespoke meaning, because inventing a feature to justify a control already on screen is the wrong way round. ToolbarControlsTests' deferred set is now empty and kept as a named empty set.

title: Show uncommitted state as a marker column, not a row tint
description:
Replace the uncommitted-row background tint with a narrow marker column that
shows `-`, `*` or `+` for a bead that is deleted, modified or new relative to
`HEAD`.

## Today

`BeadRowView.drawBackground` (`Sources/VBXUI/BeadTable.swift`) fills the whole
row with `controlAccentColor` at 12% alpha when
`uncommittedReason(row.id) != nil`, wired up in `IssueListView` via
`store.dirtyBeads.reason(for:)`.

A tint over the entire row is a lot of visual weight for a small fact, it
competes with the alternating stripe and with selection (the tint is suppressed
while selected, so a selected dirty row loses the signal entirely), and it
cannot distinguish the three cases `BeadDirtyState` already keeps apart.

## Wanted

- Drop the row-background tint; `BeadRowView`'s `isUncommitted` drawing goes
  away with it (keep the row view only if something else still needs it).
- Add a very small column immediately **before** the ID column, drawing one
  character per row:
  - `+` added since the last commit
  - `*` modified since the last commit
  - `-` deleted since the last commit
  - blank when the bead is clean, and blank for every row when
    `dirtyBeads.isKnown` is false (absent, never zero — the state must not
    render as "everything clean").

## Constraints this touches

- **A column is declared once**, in `IssueListView.specs`. It is unsortable, so
  it supplies its own identifier (like the existing `type` column) rather than
  taking one from `SortColumn`; that identifier is a storage contract for saved
  layouts. Width fixed and narrow — `type` at 22/22/22 is the precedent. Decide
  whether it is `isProtected` (unhideable): the mark is the only remaining
  surface for the dirty state once the tint is gone, so protecting it is the
  likely answer.
- **Hosted cell content is aligned leading by `HostedCell`**, so the glyph does
  not need per-column alignment work — but check it does not read as
  left-jammed at that width; centring may want the cell to say so deliberately.
- **Colour alone is not an affordance** — the existing tooltip stays. The row's
  help text still comes from `BeadDirtyState.reason(for:)`, which needs a third
  case if deleted beads get a row (below).

## Open question: what row does `-` attach to?

`BeadDirtyState.removed` is documented as having *no row to mark* — the bead is
gone from disk, so nothing in `store.visibleIssues` represents it. As things
stand a `-` glyph has nowhere to render. Two ways out, and this needs a call
before implementing:

1. **Surface removed beads as rows** synthesised from the `snapshot_at` `HEAD`
   read that `BeadDirtyState.compare` already performs — a row whose fields come
   from the committed record, marked `-`, and presumably not editable. Truthful,
   and it is the case most worth seeing, but it means rows that no longer exist
   in the workspace flowing through filtering, sorting, metrics and the detail
   pane.
2. **Ship `+` and `*` only**, and leave deletions to the "N uncommitted" summary
   in `ContentView`, which already counts them.

Option 1 is what the request asks for; option 2 is the smaller change. Either
way the choice belongs in the commit message, and in an ADR note if rows are
synthesised.

## Tests

- `Tests/VBXUITests/UncommittedBeadsTests.swift` renders a row with
  `isUncommitted` true/false and asserts an ink difference. That assertion is
  about the tint and has to be rewritten against the marker column.
- The `Table columns` test asserts the identifier/`SortColumn` contract; the new
  unsortable column must satisfy it.
- Add coverage that a clean workspace and an *unknown* dirty state both render a
  blank marker, since those are the two ways a wrong signal is invisible.
close_reason: Shipped: + and * gutter column before the ID, replacing the row tint. The - case is deferred to vbx-iyy, which carries the decision.

title: Decide whether a deleted bead gets a row, so the gutter can draw -
description:
Decide whether a bead deleted since the last commit gets a row in the list, so
the uncommitted gutter can draw `-` for it.

Deferred out of `vbx-r0m`, which shipped `+` and `*`. The gutter has no `-`
because a deleted bead is gone from disk: `BeadDirtyState.removed` holds its id,
but nothing in `store.visibleIssues` represents it, so there is no row to mark.
Today a deletion shows up only in the toolbar's "N uncommitted" count, which has
always included it.

## What surfacing them would mean

`BeadDirtyState.compare` already reads the committed set through the engine's
`snapshot_at`, so the *records* are in hand and are thrown away. Keeping them
and injecting the removed ones back into the list is the easy half. The hard
half is that such a row is not a bead the workspace has:

- **No metrics.** `GraphMetrics` is computed over the beads on disk, so blocks,
  blocked-by and PageRank are absent — not zero. The row has to render them the
  way an unavailable metric renders everywhere else.
- **Every edit must refuse.** Priority and title editing write through `br`,
  which has nothing to write to. A refusal needs a reason, in the same shape as
  `editingUnavailableReason`.
- **It is not only the list.** The board, graph, tree and the detail pane all
  read the same beads. A row that exists in one surface and not the others is
  its own kind of wrong, so this is a decision about the data the store
  publishes, not about a column.
- **Filtering and sorting** run over it like any other row, including recipes
  and hybrid search, which rank ids the engine returned — and the engine does
  not know this bead exists.

## The alternative

Leave the list alone and give deletions their own surface — the toolbar count is
already there, and a popover listing what a commit would remove would answer the
question without inventing rows. Cheaper, and it does not put a bead that is not
in the workspace in front of every feature that reads the workspace.

Whichever way it goes, ADR-015's "three cases, not one" consequence and the note
on `BeadDirtyState.removed` both need updating to match.
close_reason: Decided: no synthesised rows for deleted beads. A deletion is named in the status-bar summary instead. Recorded in ADR-015.

title: docs/html goes stale on release: nothing regenerates it
description:
`docs/html/` is generated from `docs/*.md`, but nothing regenerates it when a
release rewrites `docs/RELEASES.md`. So the committed HTML silently falls behind
the Markdown it is generated from.

Found while implementing `vbx-r0m`: running `scripts/build-docs.py` for an
unrelated edit to `VBX_DESIGN.md` also rewrote `RELEASES.html`, which was
missing **0.1.2 and 0.1.3** — both released earlier the same day. Nobody had
regenerated it since 0.1.1, and nothing would have.

`.github/workflows/release.yml` calls `scripts/release-notes.py`, which writes
`docs/RELEASES.md` and commits it. It does not run `scripts/build-docs.py`, so
the HTML for the page whose whole purpose is listing releases is the one page
guaranteed to go stale.

## Options

1. **Regenerate in the release workflow** — call `build-docs.py` after
   `release-notes.py` and include `docs/html/` in the same commit. Keeps the
   committed HTML true, at the cost of a bigger release commit.
2. **A `--check` in the verify block** — `build-docs.py --check` failing when
   the HTML differs from what the Markdown would produce. Catches every source
   of drift rather than just this one, and matches how `build-engine.sh`,
   `build-icon.sh` and `build-notices.py` already work. Does not fix the release
   path on its own: the workflow commits without running the verify block.
3. **Both**, which is probably the answer — (2) makes the drift visible
   anywhere, (1) stops the one case that produces it unattended.

Note the released HTML is only as current as the last person to run the script,
so whichever option lands should also regenerate once to clear the backlog.
close_reason: Fixed: build-docs.py --check in the verify block, and version-bump.sh regenerates docs/html when it records a release.

title: Halve the uncommitted gutter and right-align its mark
description:
Halve the uncommitted gutter — the `+` / `*` column before the ID — and align
its glyph to the trailing edge, so the mark sits against the ID it belongs to
rather than floating at the far left of the window.

Shipped in `vbx-r0m` at a fixed 20pt, aligned leading like every other hosted
column.

## What to change

- `IssueListView.specs`: the `dirtyMarkID` spec goes from `width: 20,
  minWidth: 20, maxWidth: 20` to 10pt on all three. It stays fixed-width;
  a gutter that resizes is not a gutter.
- The glyph draws right-aligned instead of leading.

## Two constraints that make this more than two numbers

**10pt of column is 2pt of content.** `HostedCell` pins its hosting view to
both cell edges with a 4pt inset each side, so a 10pt column leaves 2pt to draw
in and the character clips or disappears. Whatever lands here has to give the
inset back — a per-column inset on the spec, or a narrower one for this column —
and the answer should be checked against a rendered cell, not reasoned about:
the glyph is a monospaced callout character, wider than 2pt on its own.

**Leading alignment is applied once, on purpose.** `HostedCell.host(_:)` wraps
every hosted view in `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, alignment: .leading)`, and
CLAUDE.md records why: the hosting view is pinned to both edges, so content
handed the full column width centres itself, and that put *every* hosted column
in the middle of its cell after the move to `NSTableView`. It is applied in one
place so a new column cannot forget it.

So this column needs a way to say "trailing" without reopening that hole. The
obvious shape is an alignment on `BeadColumnSpec` defaulting to `.leading`,
which `HostedCell` reads — one place still decides, and the default keeps every
existing column exactly as it is. Anything that instead alignment-wraps inside
the column's own content re-creates the bug the rule exists to prevent, and
should be rejected in review.

## Tests

- `Cell alignment` measures where ink starts in a column as a fraction of the
  cell's width, and asserts `< 0.25` for leading columns. It needs the mirror
  assertion for this one — ink starting *late* in its cell — and the existing
  leading assertions must keep passing, since the point is that the default did
  not move.
- The rendered-cell tests in `Uncommitted beads` should still show ink at 10pt;
  a clipped glyph is the failure mode this bead is most likely to ship, and
  `inkCoverage` scoped to the cell is what catches it.
- `Table columns` asserts each column has a usable width range, so the new
  min/width/max must stay consistent.

Cosmetic, but check the result against a real render rather than a build that
compiles: at this size the difference between "tight" and "clipped" is a couple
of points.
close_reason: Shipped: gutter is 10pt with the mark on the trailing edge; alignment and inset are declared on BeadColumnSpec and applied by HostedCell.

title: Refuse edits to closed beads, which are immutable
description:
A closed bead is a record of what happened. Editing one rewrites history rather
than tracking work, so vbx should not offer the edit at all — not offer it and
then fail, and not offer it and succeed.

## Where editing happens today

Two surfaces, and they need different answers:

- **Title** — `IssueListView.swift:142`, an in-place field editor opened by
  double-clicking the title cell, committing through `store.setTitle(_:for:)`.
  One bead at a time.
- **Priority** — `IssueListView.swift:340`, committing through
  `store.setPriority(_:for:)`, which takes a **`Set<Issue.ID>`**. It applies to
  the whole selection, so a selection mixing open and closed beads is the case
  that has to be decided rather than discovered.

Both end at `BeadWriter`, which shells out to `br update`.

## What "not possible" should mean

Refusing at the point of the write is the least of it — by then the user has
typed a new title and pressed Return, and the edit vanishing with an error is a
worse experience than never having opened the editor. The double-click should
not open the field editor on a closed bead in the first place, and the priority
command should be disabled when the selection is closed.

**Mixed selection** is the decision to make. Applying to the open beads and
silently skipping the closed ones is the kind of partial success that is only
noticed later; refusing the whole command is easier to reason about but
irritating on a large selection. Whichever is chosen, the result must be
visible — a disabled command with a reason, or a count of what was skipped.

**Colour alone is not an affordance**, per the accessibility bead already open,
so "you cannot edit this" needs to be legible without relying on the row looking
different. A tooltip on the refused affordance is the cheap version.

## Open question: does `br` already refuse?

Unverified, and it changes the shape of the fix. If `br update` rejects a write
to a closed issue, vbx is aligning with the engine and the UI gate is a courtesy
that turns an error into an absent affordance. If `br` accepts it, the rule is
vbx's own — and gating only the UI leaves it unenforced everywhere else, which
is worth saying out loud rather than leaving implied.

Worth checking against a scratch workspace rather than the demo fixture, which
must stay writable by `br` (see CLAUDE.md).

## Reopening

Out of scope, but it is the obvious next question and the reason this is not
simply "closed beads are read-only forever": the escape hatch for a bead closed
by mistake is to reopen it, and then it is editable again because it is no
longer closed. That keeps the rule a function of status rather than a separate
lock, and means nothing new has to be stored.

## Tests

- The pure part: given a closed bead, the title cell reports itself
  non-editable, and the priority command reports itself disabled. Given an open
  one, both are available — the check must not be a wall.
- Mixed selection resolves to whatever is decided above, asserted explicitly
  rather than falling out of the implementation.
- Note a synthetic click cannot activate anything inside the table (CLAUDE.md),
  so assert the state either side of the click — `isEditable` on the field, the
  command's enabled state — not "the double-click did nothing", which passes
  either way.
